title: Perceived well-being and light-reactive hormones: An exploratory study
research_question: To identify lighting conditions of office workplaces that favour productivity and well-being by finding congruent relationships between objective (melatonin, cortisol) and subjective (transitory mood, somnolence, visual comfort) measurements in response to light stimuli. A secondary aim was to test the importance of co-variables such as individuals' previous exposure to daylight (photic history) and psychological profile (personality type, perceived stress, emotional state).

participants.description: 4 males and 3 females, mean age = 31 years (SD = 8.7 years). Participants were screened to rule out severe vision disabilities, infections, extreme chronotypes, and endocrinology disturbances.
participants.recruitment: Subjects were invited for an introduction at the laboratory to be informed about the aims and procedure of the experiment.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two simulated office workplaces, each with two lighting systems: 1) general lighting from three 36W compact fluorescent lamps (CFLs) and 2) wall-washing lighting from three LED tubes (20W, 21W, 24W). Four experimental conditions were created by combining two CCTs (3000 K or 4000 K) and two light levels (lower: CFL only, ~450 lx desktop; higher: CFL + LED wall wash, ~800 lx desktop). The LED system at higher light levels expanded the blue component (415-480 nm) even in 3000K CCT. Melanopic illuminance ranged from 1.78 lx to 8.86 lx.

Two categorized questions on time spent under natural light
Self-report questions on nocturnal sleep hours (working week and weekends)
Four basic emotional qualities (activation, orientation, evaluation, control) on 12 four-grade rating scales
Comparison and error correction task (lists of numbers/letters)

mechanisms: The spectral blue component of light (especially 4000K CCT and LED system) promotes ipRGC photoreception, which is involved in non-image-forming processes and visual functions.
Psychological profile (e.g., perceived stress, personality type) mediates the relationship between environmental stimuli and human responses.
Melatonin and cortisol patterns behave in a complementary way (high melatonin/low cortisol at night, vice versa during day).
Light's intensity and spectral composition have an acute suppressive effect on melatonin secretion.
Cool white LED light with significant short-wavelength output is likely to elicit alertness because melatonin is more susceptible to suppression in this region.
The circadian stimulus (CS) value relates to melatonin suppression.
Quality of mood tends to reflect the level of alertness: increased sleepiness declines mood and impairs concentration/memory.
moderators: Individuals' psychological profile (personality type, perceived stress, emotional state)
implementation_implications: Lighting designers should better understand the psychobiological resources they are manipulating.
Office lighting conditions should favour productivity and well-being.
Suitable lighting designs (lamps, luminaires, light level, spatial distribution, colour appearance) need to be identified for health and well-being.
Consider the individuals' psychological profile in lighting practice, as it might explain vulnerability to light (e.g., in SAD).
Optimal lighting should provide visual performance, visual comfort, aesthetic appreciation, and energy conservation, while also supporting comfort and health.
Lighting in office spaces must meet task demands, comfort, and health.
The study contributes to identifying optimal lighting for visual comfort, perception of space, and ipRGC photoreception.
The CCTs (3000K and 4000K) and light levels (450lx to 800lx) used have the potential to impact psychobiological parameters relevant to office workers' well-being, mediated by personal resources.

limitations: The study is a pilot study with inherent limitations.
Limited exposure time (1.5 hours per condition) may not be sufficient for acute suppressive hormonal effects.
Limited range of CCTs used (3000K and 4000K) may not capture broader effects.
Small sample size (N=7) limits generalizability and statistical power.
Experiments were carried out during the morning, making cortisol a more reliable indicator than melatonin for testing hypotheses.

The Circadian Stimulus (CS) metric used is incomplete, as it does not consider timing, duration, distribution, photic history, or the spectral and absolute sensitivity of non-visual alerting effects of light exposure.

paper_metadata.title: Perceived well-being and light-reactive hormones: An exploratory study
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Perceived well-being and light-reactive hormones: An exploratory study
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Light can impact psychobiological processes in a healthy or harmful way, challenging designers to better understand the resources they are manipulating. The present exploratory study compared two forms of office lighting which differed in correlated colour temperatures and light level. A holistic approach, comprising visual, emotional and biological dimensions, was used to assess the lighting conditions that could favour productivity and well-being by means of the identification of congruent relationships between objective and subjective measurements in response to light stimuli. The former included analyses of melatonin and cortisol, and the latter were psychological instruments for measuring transitory mood, somnolence, and visual comfort. Controlled experiments were run in a laboratory with a repeated measures design, which yielded fifty-six evaluations. Although no extreme ranges of correlated colour temperatures were used in this study, the spectral blue component present in the correlated colour temperature of approximately 4000 K, and also provided by the light-emitting diodes system at a higher light level, could have contributed to render most of the strong effects on the inter and intra correlations among the psychobiological responses. The mediator role of the psychological profile of the individuals was demonstrated by the significant predictive value of the perceived stress measures.

environmental_features: Lighting with specific Correlated Color Temperatures (CCTs)
control_conditions: Different CCTs and illuminance levels served as comparison conditions

theory_commitments.theory_name: Non-visual effects of light on human physiology
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Light exposure, particularly its spectral composition and intensity, influences human circadian rhythms, hormone secretion (e.g., melatonin), and subjective well-being independently of visual perception.

mechanism_chain.description: Exposure to specific light conditions activates non-visual photoreceptors, leading to modulation of the circadian system and subsequent changes in hormone levels, which in turn affect perceived well-being.

steps.to_construct: Activation of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)
Signal transmission to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)
Changes in alertness and perceived well-being
